focus_areas: Held capacity versus progress in the Llama 3 405B run
The three places a job loses capacity, in the order it meets them
Allocated capacity as the start of the accounting, not evidence of use
The serving replica's boundary test (a loss that remains with requests switched off)
rationale.question_strategy: Estimate the Llama 3 held-to-progress fraction in an MCQ, name the three loss places in a SHORT question, apply the serving boundary test in an MCQ, correct the allocation-equals-use misconception in a TF question, and sequence a job's life against the boundaries in an ORDER question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Quantitative estimate -> conceptual decomposition -> boundary classification -> misconception check -> sequencing.
rationale.integration: Opens the chapter's accounting by contrasting what orchestration dashboards report with what becomes useful work, using the running Llama 2 70B job and its serving twin.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Framing section that motivates the goodput accounting used in every later section.

questions.question: Meta's Llama 3 405B run kept more than 90% of its elapsed time as effective training time and ran its kept steps at about 41% MFU. What does multiplying the two figures show about where its held capacity went?
choices: Roughly 90% became progress, because MFU describes kernel quality and does not reduce useful output
Roughly 41% became progress, because effective training time already includes the MFU loss
Roughly 37% became progress, and most of the loss came from the hundreds of unexpected interruptions the job survived
Roughly 37% of the peak-rate capacity it held became training progress, and most of the loss came from kept steps running below the hardware's rate rather than from interruptions
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The product $0.90 \times 0.41 \approx 0.37$ is the share of held peak-rate capacity that became progress. Interruptions cost at most a tenth of held time, while the kept steps left more than half of their capacity unused, so one of the most carefully engineered runs on record lost most of its gap to steps that ran below the hardware's rate. The product is only an estimate, because the two figures come from different measurement windows.
questions.learning_objective: Estimate the share of held capacity that becomes progress from effective training time and MFU, and identify where most of the loss lies.

questions.question: Name the three places a fleet job can lose capacity, in the order the job meets them, and explain why a dashboard that counts allocated accelerators as used cannot see most of them.
questions.answer: First, before the job holds a complete allocation: capacity that sits unallocated, is fragmented where no queued group fits, or is held by a group still waiting for its remaining members produces nothing. Second, while it holds devices without keeping progress: startup, input waits, checkpoint pauses, recovery, and rework leave no retained step. Third, inside kept steps that run below the hardware's rate because of exposed communication, stragglers, memory stalls, or long chains of small kernels. An allocation dashboard counts a partial group as allocated and every held hour as used, so it misses the partial-group loss and all of the second and third losses.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the three places fleet capacity is lost and why allocation accounting cannot see them.

questions.question: The chapter counts a serving replica's loss in its accounting only if the loss would remain with the request stream switched off. Which loss belongs to the serving analysis instead?
choices: Time the replica spends loading weights and warming up before it serves
A decode step that streams weights more slowly than the node's memory bandwidth allows
A request that waits behind a long batch because requests arrive unevenly
Capacity the replica holds in reserve for bursts, running below its ideal rate
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. A request waiting behind a long batch exists only because arrivals are uneven, so it fails the boundary test and belongs to serving. Weight loading and warmup, a decode step below its bandwidth limit, and reserved headroom all remain with requests switched off, so they are counted here, averaged over windows of hours to weeks. How much headroom a latency target requires is still a serving decision.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the boundary test that separates fleet-efficiency losses from serving losses.

questions.question: True or False: A shared fleet whose accelerators are fully allocated is, by that fact, using its capacity well, so fleet efficiency accounting can start from the busy count.
questions.answer: False. Allocated capacity is where the accounting of fleet efficiency starts, not evidence that the capacity was used well. Devices can be held by a group still waiting for its remaining members, held by a job that is starting up or recovering, or busy in steps that run far below the hardware's rate. The orchestrator's accounting separates allocated from productive capacity but cannot say where inside a job the missing work went.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish allocated capacity from capacity that becomes useful work.

questions.question: Order the following events in the life of the running example's training job, from first to last: (1) its kept steps run below the hardware's rate because collectives are exposed, (2) its group of 16 nodes becomes a complete allocation, (3) it waits in the queue while other teams' jobs hold the capacity, (4) it starts up, compiles, and loads its initial state before the first step.
questions.answer: The correct order is (3) -> (2) -> (4) -> (1). The queue wait comes first and, while other jobs hold the capacity, costs only time to result. Formation of the complete allocation is the first boundary, after which startup and compilation consume held time without retained steps, a runtime loss. Only then do kept steps run, and their exposed collectives are a program loss. The order matters because each factor divides by what the previous boundary passed.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence a job's life against the scheduling, runtime, and program boundaries.

focus_areas: ML productivity goodput as the product of scheduling, runtime, and program goodput
Loss shares weighted by what earlier boundaries passed
MFU as program goodput only over retained steps; MBU for bandwidth-bound decode
Charging each loss at the first boundary it fails to cross
rationale.question_strategy: Compute the Llama 3 loss split in an MCQ, interpret MFU against MBU for decode in an MCQ, explain the double-counting trap of run-averaged MFU in a SHORT question, correct the straggler-charging misconception in a TF question, recall the named ideal in a FILL question, and classify checkpoint and compilation losses in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Quantitative decomposition -> metric selection -> denominator reasoning -> boundary rule -> definition recall -> classification.
rationale.integration: Turns the three loss places into one accounting whose factors multiply, and connects MFU and MBU to program goodput.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core definitional section; every later section measures, attributes, or trades the factors defined here.

questions.question: Applying the loss-share decomposition to Llama 3 405B on its dedicated cluster (scheduling goodput 1, runtime goodput about 0.90, program goodput about 0.41), which split of its held capacity is correct?
choices: About 10% lost at the runtime boundary, 53% at the program boundary, and 37% becoming progress at the ideal rate
About 10% lost at the runtime boundary, 59% at the program boundary, and 31% becoming progress, because each factor's loss is charged against full capacity
About 59% lost at the runtime boundary and 10% at the program boundary, because the program factor is measured first
About 37% lost at the runtime boundary, 41% at the program boundary, and 22% becoming progress
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. With scheduling goodput of one, the runtime share is $1 - 0.90 = 0.10$, the program share is the program loss weighted by what the runtime boundary passed, $0.90 \times 0.59 \approx 0.53$, and useful work is $0.90 \times 0.41 \approx 0.37$; the three parts add to one. Charging the program's 59% loss against full capacity subtracts the runtime loss twice. Removing every interruption could therefore recover at most a tenth of the held capacity, while the program boundary held most of the gap.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the loss-share decomposition to split a gap in useful work among the goodput factors.

questions.question: A serving replica's batch-one decode step reports an MFU of 2.5% and a model bandwidth utilization (MBU) of 86%. How should these figures be read when assigning the replica's program goodput?
choices: The accelerators are faulty, because an MFU this low cannot occur on a healthy device

The step is memory-saturated rather than inefficient; for bandwidth-bound decode the named ideal is the bandwidth floor, so program goodput is MBU, and the low MFU reflects a batch size that serving sets
Program goodput is 2.5%, because MFU is the only measure of program goodput that composes across workloads
Program goodput is about 44%, the average of the two, so training and decode can share one program factor
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Small-batch decode must read every weight to perform a few operations per weight, so memory bandwidth sets its time and the arithmetic units run far below peak. Charging that gap to the program would assign it a loss no program change can recover, since only a larger batch, a serving decision, raises the work done per byte. Against the bandwidth floor, program goodput is MBU, and high MBU with low MFU marks a memory-saturated program. Ideals that measure different resources cannot be averaged; a fleet report carries program goodput per workload class or converts every class to the arithmetic ideal and attributes decode's loss to batch size.
questions.learning_objective: Select the named ideal for program goodput and interpret MFU and MBU for bandwidth-bound decode.

questions.question: A team multiplies a published MFU averaged over a whole run by a runtime goodput computed from the same run's restart and checkpoint logs. Why does this product understate the job's goodput, and over what must MFU be measured for it to equal program goodput?
questions.answer: A run-averaged MFU divides by elapsed time that already includes restarts and checkpoint pauses, so those losses sit inside the MFU and the runtime factor charges them again. The product is valid only when each factor divides by exactly what the previous one passed, so that each numerator cancels the next denominator. MFU equals program goodput when it is measured over the steps that runtime goodput retained, with input waits already removed, against the time the required operations would take at peak.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how overlapping denominators double-count losses and when MFU equals program goodput.

questions.question: True or False: A straggling rank that slows every synchronous step should be charged to runtime goodput, because the reliability layer is the one that decides whether to replace the node.
questions.answer: False. The boundary decides where a loss is counted, and the cause decides who fixes it. The job holds a complete allocation and keeps every step, but those steps run below their ideal, so the straggler is a program goodput loss. Charging it there makes program goodput fall when the straggler appears and recover when the node is replaced, while the replacement decision stays with the reliability layer, which weighs that gain against the runtime goodput a restart costs.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the first-boundary rule to charge a straggler's cost to the correct factor.

questions.question: Program goodput is the ratio of the retained steps' ____ execution time to their actual execution time, so code, compiler, and communication inefficiency are charged against a named reference.
questions.answer: ideal. For arithmetic-bound training and prefill steps, the ideal is the time to perform the model's required operations at peak rate, which makes program goodput equal to MFU; for bandwidth-bound decode it is the bandwidth floor, which makes it MBU.
questions.learning_objective: Recall the definition of program goodput and its named ideal.

questions.question: Which assignment of losses to goodput factors follows the chapter's accounting boundaries?
choices: Synchronous checkpoint pause: program; asynchronous checkpoint writes that contend with the step: runtime; compilation before the first step: program
Synchronous checkpoint pause: scheduling; asynchronous checkpoint writes: runtime; compilation before the first step: scheduling
All three: runtime, because the fault-tolerance and compiler layers rather than the model cause them
Synchronous checkpoint pause: runtime; asynchronous checkpoint writes that contend with the step: program; compilation before the first step: runtime
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. A synchronous pause stops the step while the job holds its devices, so the interval produces no retained step and is a runtime loss. Asynchronous writes let steps continue but contend with them for memory and network bandwidth, lengthening retained steps, a program loss. Compiling before the first step is startup, a runtime loss, while the speed of the compiled code is program goodput. Preemption follows the same logic: the orchestrator decides it, yet the lost work and the reload are runtime losses because the job held its allocation when they occurred.
questions.learning_objective: Classify checkpoint and compilation losses by the first accounting boundary they fail to cross.

focus_areas: The measurement contract and its per-factor window
Localizing a loss with scheduler records, job timelines, and step traces
Fleet profiling by always-on metrics, targeted traces, and stratified sampling
Regression tiers by goodput factor
rationale.question_strategy: Order the localization records, test the per-factor window in an MCQ, identify the canary tier in an MCQ, analyze gray-failure amplification and trace-volume scaling in SHORT questions, and check the software-version field of the contract in a TF question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Evidence ordering -> window reasoning -> regression tier selection -> straggler mechanics -> sampling design -> contract field check.
rationale.integration: Makes the factors measurable and comparable across time, versions, and jobs on a shared fleet.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Methodology section that every later attribution and lever decision depends on.

questions.question: Order the three records used to localize a goodput shortfall, from first consulted to last: (1) step traces from selected ranks over a short window, (2) the job timeline from the gang-complete timestamp to release, (3) scheduler records of allocation intervals and gang-complete times.
questions.answer: The correct order is (3) -> (2) -> (1). Scheduler records cover every job at no extra cost and settle scheduling goodput, but cannot see inside a held allocation. The job timeline settles runtime goodput and detects, without explaining, retained steps that run slower than planned. Step traces are costly, perturb the step, and cover only their window, so they are collected only after the cheaper records show that the retained steps themselves are slow. A trace taken first can call a job healthy while it loses a third of its held time to restarts that no trace window contained.
questions.learning_objective: Order the localization records and explain what each can and cannot establish.

questions.question: A team measures runtime goodput over one day in which no failure occurs and reports a value near one. Why does the measurement contract reject this as the job's runtime goodput?
choices: Runtime goodput can be measured only on a dedicated allocation, so any shared-fleet measurement is invalid
Runtime goodput is defined only over warmed steady-state steps, so a one-day window contains too much startup
Runtime goodput charges rare, costly events such as failures that discard the steps since the last checkpoint, so its window must span many interruptions, which at fleet scale means days to weeks
Runtime goodput follows the daily demand cycle, so it must be measured overnight when queues drain
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. A window shorter than the interval between failures can show almost no runtime loss; the running example on 128 GPUs meets a hardware failure only about once every 13 days. Program goodput loses time in every step, so warmed steady-state windows estimate it well, and scheduling goodput follows demand, so its window must span whole demand cycles. The three factors multiply into the job's MPG only when they describe the same calendar window.
questions.learning_objective: Choose a measurement window that matches the rate at which each goodput factor loses time.

questions.question: Which regression tier is designed to catch a code change that looks harmless on one GPU but bends the scaling efficiency curve before a full-fleet launch?
choices: Small-scale canaries that measure step time and MFU on one node and on a small multi-node allocation
Startup and recovery baselines kept in the job timelines
Allocation baselines kept in the scheduler records over whole demand cycles
Single-GPU unit tests run with debug assertions enabled
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. A program regression slows every step, so it shows up on a small allocation within minutes. Startup and recovery baselines watch runtime goodput, such as a compiler upgrade that adds minutes to every startup while leaving step time unchanged, and allocation baselines watch scheduling goodput across whole demand cycles. A single-GPU test cannot observe the collectives and synchronization that change with scale.
questions.learning_objective: Match a regression to the testing tier and record that can detect it.

questions.question: In a synchronous data-parallel job on 1,000 GPUs, explain why one gray-failure node that delivers 10% less throughput can lower the whole job's MFU by about 10%, which goodput factor the loss is charged to, and what always-on evidence exposes it.
questions.answer: Every rank must finish before a synchronized step advances, so a rank running at 90% of its normal throughput sets the step time of every rank that waits for it, and the job runs near 90% of its former rate when that rank lies on the critical path. The job still holds a complete allocation and keeps every step, so the loss is charged to program goodput, in the Fleet Law's synchronization term. Per-rank step timers and the fleet-wide step-time distribution expose the slow rank, and a timer past its threshold triggers a trace of that rank beside a healthy peer.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how barrier synchronization turns one slow node into a job-wide program goodput loss and how it is detected.

questions.question: A 5-second Nsight Systems trace of one GPU occupies about 500 MB. Using the scaling of that trace to 1,024 GPUs, explain why production fleets pair always-on metrics with targeted or sampled traces, and name one coverage rule a sampling policy must follow.
questions.answer: The same window across 1,024 GPUs produces about 512 GB, a rate no fleet can store or read continuously, and recording every launch perturbs the step it measures. Fleets therefore keep cheap always-on measures for every job, such as step time, MFU of retained steps, per-rank step timers, and device telemetry, to detect that a factor moved, then capture short traces from ranks chosen to test a hypothesis. Samples must be stratified across jobs, parallel groups, pipeline stages, step phases, and hours of the day rather than drawn only from rank 0 or a job's first minutes, and rare events need threshold-triggered capture.
questions.learning_objective: Justify hierarchical fleet profiling from trace-volume scaling and state a sampling coverage rule.

questions.question: True or False: Because a before-and-after measurement of one job runs on identical hardware, it isolates the effect of the change under test even if a framework or compiler upgrade occurred between the two runs.
questions.answer: False. Software alone can move delivered performance by a large multiple on unchanged hardware. Across four MLPerf Inference rounds on the same eight-GPU DGX H100 system, GPT-J throughput rose 2.7$\times$ and Llama 2 70B 1.4$\times$ as the inference software moved from TensorRT 9.0 to 10.8. The contract therefore records software, compiler, and driver versions as part of the system state, and a measurement that spans an upgrade measures the upgrade along with the change.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why the measurement contract fixes software version as part of system state.

focus_areas: Complete allocations and the in-service denominator
Queue wait versus scheduling loss
Attributing orchestration losses by first boundary missed versus the layer that removes them
The shared-pool snapshot and the ceiling of group admission
rationale.question_strategy: Compute the snapshot's scheduling goodput and admission ceiling in an MCQ, analyze reserved-block reclamation in a SHORT question, correct the queue-wait misconception in a TF question, read scheduler records for two causes of free capacity in an MCQ, recall the availability report in a FILL question, and justify scheduler-logged completion in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Quantitative calculation -> loss movement between factors -> misconception check -> diagnostic reading -> denominator recall -> evidence design.
rationale.integration: Separates the losses scheduling goodput counts from the orchestrator's broader utilization diagnosis, leaving the levers with fleet orchestration.
rationale.ranking_explanation: First factor section; it sizes the boundary a job meets before any step runs.

questions.question: In a shared pool's snapshot, 80% of in-service capacity is assigned to jobs, 15% is held by groups still waiting for their remaining members, and 5% sits in complete allocations waiting for input. What is the pool's scheduling goodput, and how far can atomic group admission alone raise it?
choices: 0.80, rising to 0.95, because every assigned device counts as held and admission removes the input waits
0.60, rising to 0.80, because both the incomplete groups and the input waits are scheduling losses
0.65, rising at most to 0.80, and only if other jobs' complete allocations take every freed device
0.65, rising to 1.0, because group admission eliminates every interval of unheld capacity
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Scheduling goodput counts only capacity held by complete allocations, $0.80 - 0.15 = 0.65$, so the 35% loss is the 20% no job holds plus the 15% held by incomplete groups. The 5% input wait lies inside complete allocations, so it is a runtime loss. Group admission returns the 15% to the pool as free capacity, giving a ceiling of $0.65 + 0.15 = 0.80$ that is reached only if backfill and packing refill every freed device.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate a pool's scheduling goodput and the ceiling a single lever can reach.

questions.question: A team's reserved block is granted as an allocation and refused to everyone else while no job takes steps on it. Which goodput factor is charged, and why does reclaiming the block move part of the loss rather than recover all of it?
questions.answer: The block crosses the first boundary because it is held as an allocation, then fails the second because no retained step runs, so it is a runtime goodput loss. Reclaiming it recovers only the share a borrower actually uses; the share no borrower takes becomes free capacity outside any complete allocation, now a scheduling loss. A lever can move a loss between factors without removing it, and only the product shows whether the fleet gained.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how a scheduling lever can move a loss between goodput factors.

questions.question: True or False: A job's own wait in the queue always lowers its pool's scheduling goodput.
questions.answer: False. The wait lowers scheduling goodput only while capacity sat unheld during it. If other jobs held that capacity in complete allocations, the pool lost nothing, and the wait costs the job only time to result, which is weighed against goodput when factors are traded. Pushing scheduling goodput toward one lengthens such waits steeply.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish a job's queue wait from a pool's scheduling loss.

questions.question: Two pools report the same low scheduling goodput. In pool X, capacity sat free while the queue was empty; in pool Y, capacity sat free while gangs waited. Which reading of the scheduler records is correct?
choices: Both pools need a better placement policy, because scheduling goodput measures the competence of the scheduler
Pool X is larger than its demand, a capacity planning question, while pool Y has capacity stranded by placement, quota, or fragmentation, a policy question
Pool X has a fragmentation problem and pool Y has more capacity than its demand
Neither value can be interpreted without step traces from the jobs in each pool
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. A low scheduling goodput describes the pool, not its scheduler, and the same value calls for opposite remedies, so queue depth is recorded beside every interval of free capacity. Scheduler records, not step traces, settle this factor, because nothing that happens inside an allocation enters it.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret scheduler records to separate a capacity planning loss from a policy loss.

questions.question: Scheduling goodput divides by in-service capacity. Accelerators out of service for repair or maintenance are left out of the denominator, and their downtime is reported beside the product as the pool's ____.
questions.answer: availability. Dividing by installed capacity instead would fold hardware reliability into scheduling goodput, so the measurement contract records which denominator was used, and two reports that differ on it cannot be compared.
questions.learning_objective: Recall how out-of-service capacity is reported in scheduling goodput accounting.

questions.question: Why must the moment an allocation becomes complete be logged by the scheduler as an event rather than inferred from the job's first training step, and why does a serving replica make whole-node fragmentation a scheduling concern?
questions.answer: Inferring completion from the first step would move startup, a runtime loss, into the scheduling factor, so the two factors would no longer divide cleanly; startup is measured between the scheduler's gang-complete event and the timeline's first step. A serving replica is one indivisible gang, a whole node across which tensor parallelism splits the weights, so a pool can hold many free GPUs and no free node. A replica waiting for a node is a scheduling loss, while loading and warmup after placement are runtime losses.
questions.learning_objective: Justify the evidence that dates a complete allocation and apply scheduling goodput to a serving replica.

focus_areas: Retained steps at the job's fault-free step time over held time
Composing runtime loss from five owners' terms without double counting
The running example's runtime loss and which term dominates
The coupling between preemption budget and checkpoint interval; serving replica readiness
rationale.question_strategy: Read the running example's composition in an MCQ, explain the fault-free normalization in a SHORT question, apply a double-counting rule in an MCQ, correct the same-value-same-owner misconception in a TF question, recall the preemption-adjusted checkpoint interval in a FILL question, and size a serving replica's loading loss in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Quantitative composition -> boundary normalization -> composition rules -> interpretation -> coupled decision -> serving application.
rationale.integration: Places the losses priced by the storage, fault-tolerance, and orchestration chapters on one boundary so they can be compared.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Second factor section; it shows that the largest runtime lever depends on the job's size, fleet, and priority.

questions.question: The Llama 2 70B running example holds 128 GPUs for a week under a budget of one forced preemption a day. Its runtime loss terms are about 0.05% startup, 7.7% input waits, 0.4% checkpoint waste, 0.03% recovery, and 1.4% preemption. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Runtime goodput is about 0.90, and the input pipeline reaches far more held time than faster checkpoint writes and warm restart could
Runtime goodput is about 0.90, and the reliability layer owns the largest lever because checkpoint waste and recovery grow with device count
Runtime goodput is about 0.97, because preemption is charged to scheduling goodput
Runtime goodput is about 0.92, because input waits are a program loss
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The five terms add to a loss of about 10%, so runtime goodput is about 0.90, with input waits and preemption accounting for 9.1% of it. Checkpoint waste and recovery together are under half a percent, so the input pipeline reaches about 17$\times$ as much held time as recovery. Checkpoint waste and recovery grow with device count and pass input waits only near 13,000 GPUs. Preemption is a runtime loss because the job held its allocation, and input waits are carved out of the step and charged here.
questions.learning_objective: Compose a job's runtime loss from its owners' terms and identify the lever that reaches the most held time.

questions.question: Runtime goodput's numerator is the number of retained steps multiplied by the job's fault-free step time. Explain why this normalization charges a straggler that slows every step for days to program goodput, but charges the same slowdown confined to the minutes after a restart to runtime goodput.
questions.answer: The fault-free step time is the job's steady-state step time with the input batch ready and no recovery in progress, so it already contains exposed communication, pipeline bubbles, memory stalls, and a persistent straggler; those losses pass through the runtime boundary and are charged to program goodput. Steps just after a relaunch run slower because caches are cold, kernels are compiling, and the input pipeline is refilling, so their excess over the fault-free time belongs to the recovery that caused it and is a runtime loss.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how normalizing to the fault-free step time separates runtime from program losses.

questions.question: The five runtime loss terms can be added only if no interval enters two of them. Which rule keeps a failure's lost work from being counted twice?
choices: Rework is charged to both the checkpoint and failure terms, and the sum is halved
All rework is charged to the preemption term, because preemptions and failures discard work the same way
Rework is excluded entirely, because steps after the last checkpoint are neither retained nor lost
The checkpoint waste term already counts the steps a failure erases, so the failure term uses the recovery budget without rework
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Each interval is charged once. Checkpoint waste counts synchronous writes plus the expected rework after failures; a forced preemption's lost work sits in the preemption overhead; warmup belongs to the event that caused it, so the startup term counts only launches no interruption caused; the data stall ratio is a steady-state quantity; and only synchronous checkpoint pauses are runtime losses. Steps after the last commit in a window are handled by closing the window at a commit, not by excluding rework.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the composition rules that prevent an interval from entering two runtime loss terms.

questions.question: True or False: Because the running example's runtime goodput of about 0.90 matches the at least 0.90 implied for Llama 3 405B, the two jobs should call on the same owners to improve it.
questions.answer: False. The agreement hides a difference in kind. The Llama 3 run, dedicated and spread over 128$\times$ as many devices, had to hold its loss down in the failure-driven terms that grow with device count. The running example loses almost nothing there and nearly all of its loss to input waits and preemption. The same value of a factor can point to different owners, so the report carries the terms, not only their sum.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret a runtime goodput value through its composition rather than its sum.

questions.question: The running example's Young-Daly checkpoint interval of about 77 minutes was computed from hardware failures alone. Counting its budgeted preemptions as interruptions too shortens the interval to about ____ minutes.
questions.answer: 21. A forced preemption discards the work since the last checkpoint exactly as a failure does, so for choosing an interval it is another interruption. The interval belongs to the fault-tolerance layer and the preemption budget to orchestration, and only the composition shows that the two decisions are one.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize the coupling between the preemption budget and the checkpoint interval.

questions.question: A serving replica needs about 5.7 minutes to fetch, load, and warm up after it is placed. How does the replica's lifetime change this runtime loss, and what does a warm pool of loaded, idle replicas do to it?
choices: The loss is a scheduling loss because the replica cannot serve yet, so lifetime does not affect it
The loss is about 0.4% of held time for a replica released once a day and about 9% for one added for a single burst hour; a warm pool moves it to program goodput as headroom rather than removing it
The loss is the same share of held time regardless of lifetime, and a warm pool removes it entirely
The loss is charged to serving latency, so it never enters runtime goodput
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Once placed, the replica holds a complete allocation even though it cannot yet serve, so loading and warmup are runtime losses read from its lifecycle log, while provisioning precedes the complete allocation and is not charged here. Lifetime sets the share, so the capacity a fleet adds for short bursts pays the largest fraction. A warm pool keeps replicas ready but idle, which converts the loss into headroom, a program goodput loss.
questions.learning_objective: Size a serving replica's readiness loss against its lifetime and classify the effect of a warm pool.

focus_areas: Iron law terms and their mapping onto the Fleet Law
Exposed communication from one node to 128 GPUs and the scaling efficiency split
Straggler versus exposed-communication evidence in a step trace
Top-down drill-down, trace perturbation, and roofline placement by measured arithmetic intensity
rationale.question_strategy: Apply the iron law to a targeted upgrade in an MCQ, compute the scale loss and its reporting rule in an MCQ, interpret synchronized rank traces in a SHORT question, describe the drill-down in a SHORT question, place a LayerNorm kernel on the roofline in an MCQ, and distinguish measured from algorithmic intensity in a TF question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Iron law calculation -> fleet scaling calculation -> trace interpretation -> diagnostic protocol -> roofline placement -> definition check.
rationale.integration: Connects single-device iron-law reasoning to the Fleet Law terms that decide whether a local saving reaches the fleet.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Locates the largest loss inside the time the running job holds and names the term a fix must shorten.

questions.question: A training step's wall-clock time is decomposed with the iron law ($T = D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW} + O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}) + L_{\text{lat}}$) into 60% memory traffic, 30% compute, and 10% dispatch and latency overhead. A hardware upgrade doubles peak compute $R_{\text{peak}}$ while leaving memory bandwidth and overhead unchanged. What is the maximum speedup this upgrade can achieve on this workload?
choices: $2.00\times$, because doubling peak compute halves the execution time of the matrix multiplications
$1.67\times$, because the compute and overhead fractions are both accelerated by the faster arithmetic
About $1.18\times$, because doubling compute only reduces the 30% compute slice to 15% while the 70% non-compute time remains
$1.43\times$, because the memory-bound portion is compressed by the faster arithmetic units
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Doubling $R_{\text{peak}}$ affects only the compute term, halving it from 0.30 to 0.15 of the baseline time. The new normalized time is $0.60 + 0.15 + 0.10 = 0.85$, a speedup of $1/0.85 \approx 1.18\times$. A local change helps only through the term it shortens, and only by the part of that term that was exposed; expecting $2\times$ ignores that 70% of the step is governed by memory traffic and overhead.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the iron law to bound the speedup of a hardware change that shortens one term.

questions.question: The running example reaches 65% MFU on one 8-GPU node and 48% fleet MFU on 128 GPUs with the same work on each device, its step time rising from 180 ms to 245 ms. How much of the node's efficiency does scale cost, and how should a report state the job's program goodput?
choices: 17%, the direct difference in MFU points, and program goodput is $0.65 \times 0.74$ multiplied again by the fleet MFU
About 26% (a scaling efficiency of about 74%), and program goodput is either the fleet MFU of 0.48 or the node MFU times the scaling efficiency, never the fleet MFU times the scaling efficiency
About 52%, the unused share of peak, all of which is exposed communication
About 26%, and program goodput is $0.48 \times 0.74 \approx 0.36$ because the scale loss must be charged separately
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Because each device does the same work, the MFU ratio equals the step-time ratio, $180/245 \approx 0.74$, so scale costs about 26% of the node's efficiency; 17 points is an absolute difference. The fleet MFU already contains the exposed time, so multiplying it by the scaling efficiency would charge that time twice. The 65 ms added per step, about 27% of the fleet step, bounds what exposed communication and synchronization can claim, but only a step trace attributes it, since offload, kernel shapes, and barrier waits can also change between the two configurations.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the efficiency cost of scale from node and fleet MFU and report program goodput without double counting.

questions.question: Synchronized per-rank traces record the same collective in otherwise matched steps. In the baseline, every rank enters at 8 ms and all finish at 10 ms. In case A, all ranks but one enter at 8 ms, the last enters at 12 ms, and all finish at 14 ms. In case B, every rank enters at 8 ms and all finish at 14 ms. Which Fleet Law term does each case lengthen, and why do both lower the same goodput factor while pointing to different lever owners?
questions.answer: Case A adds 4 ms of waiting for one late rank while the others wait at the barrier, the signature of a straggler in the synchronization term; the next step is to trace that rank's preceding computation, input, and host work beside a healthy peer. Case B stretches the collective itself from 2 ms to 6 ms with every rank present, exposed communication in the communication term not covered by overlap. Both occur inside retained steps on a complete allocation, so both are program goodput losses. The straggler may be fixed by node replacement in the reliability layer, while exposed communication is addressed by layout and overlap. The trace localizes the interval but does not by itself prove a network fault.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose aligned-rank traces to separate a straggler from exposed communication.

questions.question: Describe the top-down drill-down from a fleet measure to a hardware root cause for a program goodput loss, and explain why the step's duration is read from the untraced job timeline rather than from the trace.
questions.answer: Fleet measures such as step time against plan, MFU of retained steps, and per-rank step timers detect the loss. Framework and distributed traces associate step time with model operations across ranks, where a lagging rank or exposed collective first appears. Kernel timelines on one rank show launch gaps and the overlap of compute and communication streams, and hardware counters report achieved bandwidth, occupancy, and instruction mix for one kernel. Each level is taken only for the ranks and window the level above selected, and the descent stops at the level that names the term. Tracing adds host work, memory, and synchronization, so a traced step can run slower or overlap differently; the trace is evidence about structure, and the duration comes from the untraced timeline.
questions.learning_objective: Synthesize the profiling hierarchy for a program goodput loss and account for trace perturbation.

questions.question: Counters for a LayerNorm kernel on an H100 report 5 TFLOP/s of achieved arithmetic and 2.8 TB/s of achieved memory bandwidth, against a peak bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s and an FP16 ridge of about 295 FLOP/byte. Which lever can deliver a material gain?
choices: Faster arithmetic units, because the kernel achieves only a tiny fraction of peak FLOP/s
A better memory schedule inside the kernel, because achieved bandwidth is far below peak
Graph replay, because a low FLOP rate always indicates host dispatch overhead
Moving fewer bytes, by fusing the normalization with the operation that produces its input or by a supported smaller representation
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Measured intensity is $5 / 2.8 \approx 1.8$ FLOP/byte, far below the ridge, so the kernel's bound lies on the bandwidth slope, and it already achieves about 83.6% of peak bandwidth. Faster arithmetic cannot raise a bandwidth ceiling, and a better schedule recovers only the small remaining gap. Fusion keeps the intermediate out of HBM. A low FLOP rate alone does not indicate dispatch, which appears instead as idle gaps between short kernels.
questions.learning_objective: Place a profiled kernel on the roofline from counter data and select the lever that can move it.

questions.question: True or False: A profiled kernel's measured arithmetic intensity always equals the algorithmic intensity of its operation, so the kernel can be placed on the roofline from the model's FLOP and byte counts alone.
questions.answer: False. Measured intensity divides the operations a kernel actually executes by the bytes observed crossing a named memory boundary, so it includes tiling, cache behavior, fusion, padding, and redundant transfers. A measured value below the algorithmic estimate exposes traffic the algorithm did not require, and a roofline point is interpretable only when its FLOP convention and memory boundary match the ceilings on the same plot.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish measured from algorithmic arithmetic intensity in roofline diagnosis.

focus_areas: Compiler-derived partitioning: annotations, propagation, and resharding collectives
Overlap of gradient exchange and contention between compute and communication streams
Readiness and lifetime obligations for multi-stream execution
Kernel-level levers by the term they shorten, and why program fixes do not add
rationale.question_strategy: Diagnose an unexpected collective after an annotation change in an MCQ, order DDP bucketed overlap, explain stream contention in a SHORT question, check producer-consumer ordering in a TF question, analyze graph replay against the decode floor in an MCQ, and reason about non-additive fixes in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Compiler mechanism -> runtime sequencing -> resource contention -> synchronization hazard -> lever reach -> composition.
rationale.integration: Recovers the program goodput loss located in the previous section through partitioning, overlap, and kernel-level levers, each judged by the Fleet Law term it shortens.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Lever section; it shows why the running job's largest program loss lies beyond the reach of kernel levers.

questions.question: In the running example, the programmer annotates the input's batch dimension along the data axis and splits the feed-forward and attention projections along the model axis. After an annotation change, a step trace shows an AllGather in every layer that the layout does not predict. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: A conflict in sharding propagation, such as a reshape or a tensor whose annotation disagrees with its neighbors, causing the compiler to insert resharding collectives that no line of the program names
The compiler has correctly added the data-parallel gradient reduction
The NVLink links are failing, so collectives are being retried
The model code contains an explicit AllGather that the annotations cannot override
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. With compiler-derived partitioning, the programmer annotates a few tensors and the compiler propagates layouts and inserts the collectives they require, such as the model-axis AllReduce after the row-split output projection. Wherever two derived layouts disagree, it inserts resharding collectives. The annotations decide which collectives exist, the mapping of the mesh onto the allocation decides how long each takes, and the overlap schedule decides how much is exposed. Counting the trace's collectives by type and mesh axis against the layout's prediction checks the propagation; the model code itself contains no collective.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose compiler-derived partitioning from the collectives a step trace shows.

questions.question: In PyTorch DistributedDataParallel, arrange the following events in the sequence that overlaps gradient communication with the backward pass: (1) the compute stream continues the backward pass on earlier layers while the bucket is transferred, (2) the backward pass computes the gradients that fill a bucket, (3) the communication stream is synchronized with the compute stream before the optimizer step, (4) a backward hook launches an asynchronous AllReduce of the bucket on a communication stream.
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) -> (4) -> (1) -> (3). A gradient bucket can be reduced as soon as the backward pass has produced it, so a hook dispatches a non-blocking AllReduce on a side stream while backward propagation continues on the main stream, and the two streams synchronize only before the optimizer step. These loose dependencies are why the data-axis exchange can be hidden, unlike model-axis AllReduce operations whose result the next operation needs.
questions.learning_objective: Order the runtime sequence of bucketed gradient overlap and explain why its dependencies allow hiding.

questions.question: Explain how a collective on a communication stream can contend with matrix multiplications on a compute stream, and state the measured condition under which overlap raises program goodput.
questions.answer: Separate streams make concurrent execution possible but do not reserve independent hardware. The collective library runs its own kernels on the same streaming multiprocessors to move and reduce data, so it competes with the matrix multiplications for those processors, memory bandwidth, and cache. On a timeline, successful overlap moves the collective's interval under computation while the compute kernels beside it grow longer. Overlap raises program goodput only if the communication time it removes from the critical path exceeds the time it adds to the computation, which only an end-to-end measurement of the step establishes.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the resource contention of concurrent compute and communication and the condition for a net gain.

questions.question: True or False: If a side-stream collective reads a tensor before its producing kernel completes, missing producer-consumer ordering can cause a data race even though each stream executes its own operations in order.
questions.answer: True. Per-stream order does not establish order between a producer on one stream and a consumer on another. Overlap that a program arranges for itself must meet two obligations a data-parallel wrapper otherwise meets for it: readiness, so that no consumer reads a tensor before its producer finishes, and lifetime, so that no tensor's storage is reused while a side stream still uses it. Both must hold before a shorter step is credited to overlap rather than to a race that skipped work.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the readiness and lifetime obligations of multi-stream execution.

questions.question: Eager submission of one forward pass of the 70B model costs roughly 12–24 ms of host time, while the serving replica's batch-one decode floor is about 5.2 ms per token. What does graph replay change, and what limits it?
choices: It fuses the pass's element-wise kernels, removing intermediate HBM traffic, and works for any input shape
It lowers the bandwidth floor of decode by keeping the weights in on-chip memory

It shortens only the host-dispatch part of the latency term by resubmitting a captured kernel sequence in one request; shapes, memory addresses, and control flow must match the capture, so varying shapes need one captured variant per shape bucket
It hides the per-layer tensor-parallel AllReduce behind computation, removing the communication term
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Because eager dispatch can exceed the bandwidth floor, eager decode can be dispatch-bound before it is bandwidth-bound, and graph replay targets exactly that interval. It does not fuse kernels or reduce bytes; fusion and tiling shorten the data term. The evidence of success is that launch gaps disappear from the kernel timeline. The replica's per-layer AllReduce, about 32.8 KB at batch one, is latency-bound and cannot be hidden because the next operation needs its result, so fewer exchanges or cheaper launches are what shorten it.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate graph replay by the term it shortens and the capture constraints that limit it.

questions.question: Two program fixes each shorten the node step when measured alone. Explain one way applying both can save less than the sum of their savings, one way it can save more, and why a fix that worked on the node baseline is measured again on the fleet configuration.
questions.answer: A lever shortens only the exposed part of its term, so after one lever runs, every term's share of the step changes. Combinations can overlap or conflict: a compiler that already fuses an element-wise chain leaves nothing for a hand-written fusion of the same chain, and a kernel speedup that shortens the backward pass shrinks the window that hid the gradient exchange, exposing communication that was free before. Combinations can reinforce: fusion and tiling free activation memory, which allows a larger microbatch that lengthens the computation available to hide each collective. On the fleet, the data-axis exchange holds most of the loss that scale adds, so only an end-to-end measurement under the contract on the fleet configuration classifies a combination.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why program fixes do not add and why each is re-measured on the fleet configuration.

focus_areas: Job product versus pool product and their loss shares
The value of one point of a factor as the product of the other two
Ranking levers by relative gain at the owners' ceilings
Cost per useful accelerator-hour and the Archetype B goodput profile
rationale.question_strategy: Compute the products and loss shares in an MCQ, value a point of program goodput in an MCQ, rank levers by ceiling in a SHORT question, price useful work in an MCQ, correct the scheduling-speeds-the-job misconception in a TF question, and apply the accounting to a recommendation fleet in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Product calculation -> marginal value -> lever ranking -> cost translation -> ownership reasoning -> archetype transfer.
rationale.integration: Composes the three sized factors into one decomposition, turns it into a lever ranking and a price, and shows the ranking is workload specific.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Synthesis section where the chapter's accounting produces decisions and costs.

questions.question: The running example has scheduling goodput 0.65, runtime goodput 0.90, and program goodput 0.48. Which statement of its products and loss shares is correct?
choices: The job product is about 0.43 and the pool's MPG about 0.28; of fleet capacity, 35% is lost to scheduling, 10% to runtime, and 52% to the program
The job product is about 0.58 and the pool's MPG about 0.43; of fleet capacity, 35%, 6%, and 15% are lost at the three boundaries
The pool's MPG is about 0.67, the average of the three factors, so a third of fleet capacity is lost
The job product is about 0.43 and the pool's MPG about 0.28; of fleet capacity, 35% is lost to scheduling, 6% to runtime, and 31% to the program
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The job product is $0.90 \times 0.48 \approx 0.43$ and the pool product is $0.65 \times 0.43 \approx 0.28$. Loss shares weight each factor's loss by what earlier boundaries passed: scheduling $1 - 0.65 = 0.35$, runtime $0.65 \times 0.10 \approx 0.06$, and program $0.59 \times 0.52 \approx 0.31$, where 0.59 is scheduling times runtime goodput. With the 0.28 that became progress, the four parts add to one. Charging the runtime and program losses against full capacity counts earlier losses again.
questions.learning_objective: Compute job and pool goodput products and the share of fleet capacity lost at each boundary.

questions.question: For the running example, what is one percentage point of program goodput worth in MPG, and why is it worth more than a point of runtime goodput?
choices: About 0.48 of a point, equal to program goodput itself
About 0.59 of a point, the product of the other two factors, $0.65 \times 0.90$; a point of runtime goodput is worth only $0.65 \times 0.48 \approx 0.31$
One full point, because MPG is the sum of the three factors
About 0.43 of a point, the job product, because scheduling goodput does not affect the program's value
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Raising one factor by a small amount raises the product by that amount times the other two. A point of program goodput is worth the most because its value is the product of the two highest factors, and a point of runtime goodput the least because its value is the product of the two lowest. Every factor's lever is worth more on a fleet whose other factors are high.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the marginal value of a goodput point as the product of the other factors.

questions.question: Scheduling loses the largest share of the running example's pool capacity, yet the chapter ranks the program lever first. Using the owners' ceilings (scheduling 0.80, runtime 0.98 with input waits removed, program 0.65 at the node baseline), explain the ranking.
questions.answer: A loss share says where capacity went, not what a lever returns, because capacity recovered at an early boundary must still cross the later ones. Each lever multiplies MPG by its factor's own relative gain: scheduling to 0.80 raises MPG about 23% to 0.35, removing input waits about 9% to 0.31, and the program to the node's 0.65 about 35% to 0.38. The program lever is worth the most because its factor has the most relative room to its ceiling. The ceilings are optimistic for every owner, but the ranking holds unless one owner's practical reach falls far below the others'.
questions.learning_objective: Rank goodput levers by relative gain at their owners' ceilings rather than by loss share.

questions.question: At an internal fleet rate of \$2 per in-service accelerator-hour, what does the running example's pool pay for one accelerator-hour of ideal-rate progress, and what does a chargeback that bills each team only for the hours it holds charge this job?
choices: About \$7.09, or 3.5$\times$ the capacity price; billing held hours charges about 2.3$\times$ the rate and leaves the scheduling loss unbilled
About \$4.17, because only program goodput divides the capacity price
About \$2.25, because only runtime losses raise the price of useful work
About \$7.09, and billing held hours charges the same 3.5$\times$, because every loss lies inside the job's allocation
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The cost of a useful accelerator-hour is the capacity price divided by MPG, about \$2 divided by 0.28, so every factor acts as a cost multiplier. A chargeback per held hour divides only by the job product of about 0.43, so the scheduling loss is billed to no one unless the cost-attribution policy assigns it. Lifting program goodput to its ceiling would cut the price of useful work by about 26% without buying an accelerator.
questions.learning_objective: Translate goodput factors into the cost of a useful accelerator-hour and evaluate a chargeback policy.

questions.question: True or False: Raising the pool's scheduling goodput is the most direct way to shorten the running example's time to result, because scheduling loses the largest share of pool capacity.
questions.answer: False. The job already holds its allocation, so the pool's unheld capacity does not slow it; capacity that a better scheduler recovers becomes complete allocations for other queued jobs. The job's product, runtime times program goodput, is what its team can change. An accounting that reports only the job's product hides the pool's largest loss from its owners, and one that reports only the pool's charges the job a loss its team cannot touch.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish what the job product and the pool product each measure and who can change them.

questions.question: For an Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) recommendation fleet, explain where a wait for embedding rows fetched from host memory and an exposed AllToAll exchange of the gathered vectors are charged, and why the running example's lever ranking cannot be reused.
questions.answer: Rows fetched ahead of the step belong to the input path, so when that path cannot keep pace with the step rate the accelerators wait for their batch, a runtime loss sized by the data stall ratio and recovered by prefetching and caching hot rows. Inside the retained step, the AllToAll's completion is set by the slowest destination under shard skew or a congested fabric, and the part the dense computation does not hide is a program loss recovered by shard balancing and message coalescing. Because such a step is bounded more by bytes moved than by arithmetic, its program goodput must name its ideal with care. The value of a point is still the product of the other two factors, but the ranking must be recomputed from that fleet's own measured factors.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the goodput accounting to a recommendation workload and justify recomputing the lever ranking.

focus_areas: The product rule for changes that touch several factors
Whose product and which window judge a trade
Compilation builds: where builds and recompilations are charged, and amortization over executions
Time to result and the efficiency frontier
rationale.question_strategy: Apply the product rule in an MCQ, calculate a compilation break-even in a SHORT question, order the compilation pipeline, classify steady-state recompilation in an MCQ, correct the job-product judgment of preemption in a TF question, and reason about time to result versus fleet goodput in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Ratio calculation -> amortization calculation -> pipeline sequencing -> boundary classification -> scope of judgment -> frontier reasoning.
rationale.integration: Turns the displacement of overhead into one decision rule across factors, then adds time to result and price to place configurations on the efficiency frontier.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Decision section that judges levers which raise one factor while lowering another.

questions.question: A change raises a job's program goodput by a tenth of its value and lowers its runtime goodput by a twelfth of its value, both measured over the same window. Does the product rise, and is scheduling goodput needed to decide?
choices: Yes; the product is multiplied by about $1.10 \times 11/12 \approx 1.008$, and scheduling goodput is not needed because an unchanged factor's ratio is one
No, because a loss in runtime goodput always outweighs an equal or larger gain in program goodput
It cannot be decided without the absolute values of scheduling and runtime goodput
Yes, by about 18%, the sum of the two percentage changes
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. A change that touches several factors multiplies MPG by the product of each factor's ratio, its value after the change divided by its value before, measured on the same boundary and window; it is worth making only when that product exceeds one. Ratios let separate owners apply the rule from their own records. The rule is asymmetric because factors start at different heights: lifting the running example's program goodput to its ceiling would still pay at up to 26% of runtime goodput, while removing every runtime loss could raise runtime goodput by only about 13%.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the product rule to decide whether a cross-factor trade raises goodput.

questions.question: A constructed 13B decode budget on one H100 runs at 120 tokens/s (8.33 ms per token): 50% matrix multiplications, 35% element-wise kernels, and 15% exposed launch overhead. Compilation leaves the matrix multiplications unchanged, removes 70% of the element-wise time and 80% of the launch overhead, and an autotuning build takes about 15 minutes. Calculate the compiled step time and speedup and the tokens needed to repay the build on one replica, and explain how sharing the artifact across 128 replicas changes the answer.
questions.answer: The compiled step is $0.50 + 0.35 \times 0.30 + 0.15 \times 0.20 = 0.635$ of the uncompiled step, about 5.3 ms per token, a 1.58$\times$ speedup that saves about 3.0 ms per token. Repaying 15 minutes takes about 300,000 tokens, roughly 26 minutes of single-stream generation. A shared artifact is repaid in about 12 seconds of the pool's generation, while per-replica builds cost about 32 GPU-hours per rollout, a quarter of the held time of a replica added for one burst hour. A build is amortized over executions, not over time.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate a compilation dividend and the executions needed to repay its build.

questions.question: Arrange the following stages of graph compilation in the order a compiler applies them: (1) fuse operations into groups whose intermediates stay on chip, (2) capture a region of the program as a graph, (3) select or generate a kernel for each fused group, (4) plan memory for the fused graph's tensors, (5) rewrite the graph with simplifications.
questions.answer: The correct order is (2) -> (5) -> (1) -> (4) -> (3). The compiler captures a region as a graph, rewrites it, fuses its operations, plans its memory across the fused graph, and finally selects or generates a kernel for each fused group. This work is paid before the first step it improves and again at every recompilation, a runtime goodput cost, while the speed of the compiled steps is program goodput.
questions.learning_objective: Order the stages of graph compilation and relate them to the two factors a build touches.

questions.question: A job's input shapes vary so much that its compiled graph recompiles every few hundred steps during steady operation. Where is that recompilation charged, and what is the remedy?
choices: Runtime goodput, as startup; the remedy is a faster compiler
Program goodput, because it recurs inside the job's own fault-free step rate and shows up as slow steps; the remedy is a compilation that accepts the shape distribution
Scheduling goodput, because the job cannot take steps while it recompiles
Nowhere, because compilation is a one-time cost paid before the first step
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. A build at a job's start, after a restart, or after a resize to a new mesh happens once per launch and is charged to runtime goodput with that launch's startup. A recompilation triggered repeatedly during steady operation lowers program goodput instead. A narrow shape range runs faster but rebuilds on new shapes, while symbolic dimensions accept varied batches and sequence lengths without rebuilding; graph breaks also split the regions a compiler can fuse and can force recompilation.
questions.learning_objective: Charge a compilation cost to the correct factor and choose the matching remedy.

questions.question: True or False: A priority preemption that lets an urgent gang form without draining capacity for it should be judged by the product of the urgent job's factors, since that job is the one the policy serves.
questions.answer: False. A lever that moves capacity between jobs also changes other jobs' factors. The urgent job gains scheduling goodput while every victim loses runtime goodput, multiplied by any cascade, so only the pool's product contains both the gain and the cost. The preemption budget sets the rate at which one is exchanged for the other.
questions.learning_objective: Determine whose product judges a lever that moves capacity between jobs.

questions.question: Time to result is the queue wait plus the job's ideal-rate accelerator-time divided by its device count times its runtime and program goodput. Explain why scheduling goodput does not appear in this relation, why holding a job to fewer devices can raise the fleet's goodput while lengthening that job's time to result, and why the product rule alone cannot choose between such configurations.
questions.answer: The pool's unallocated capacity does not slow a job that already holds its allocation, so the pool enters only through the queue wait. Program goodput falls as the device count grows, by the scaling efficiency of the layout, so adding devices shortens held time only while device count times program goodput keeps rising, and each added device lowers the pool's goodput; in the elastic example, efficiency relative to 128 GPUs is 90% at 256 and 80% at 512. The product contains no time, so two configurations with the same product can finish days apart. A deadline-driven job buys time with more devices at lower program goodput, and a fleet with a deep queue buys goodput by holding the job to fewer, points on the efficiency frontier where none dominates.
questions.learning_objective: Use the time-to-result relation to explain the trade between a job's deadline and fleet goodput on the efficiency frontier.

focus_areas: High MFU versus fleet-level goodput
Peak FLOP/s versus the exposed term of a step
Mean step time versus the step-time distribution
Compilation as hypothesis; largest loss versus largest recoverable gain
rationale.question_strategy: Expose the high-MFU fallacy in an MCQ, apply the iron law to a peak-FLOP/s upgrade in an MCQ, refute the precision-halves-the-step claim in a TF question, explain intermittent stragglers in a SHORT question, check compilation claims in an MCQ, and correct the fix-the-largest-loss fallacy in a SHORT question.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Single-factor fallacy -> term reasoning -> precision nuance -> distribution reasoning -> verification discipline -> lever valuation.
rationale.integration: Each misconception reads one factor, window, or kernel as the whole product; the questions return each to the chapter's accounting.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Synthesis section exposing common traps in fleet efficiency claims.

questions.question: A team reports that its job's retained steps run at 48% MFU, above the 41% of Llama 3 405B, and concludes that the job uses the fleet well. Why is the conclusion unsupported?
choices: MFU above 45% is not achievable on these accelerators, so the measurement must be wrong
MFU overstates program goodput because it counts recomputation as useful work
MFU measures only program goodput; with the pool's scheduling goodput of 0.65 and the job's runtime goodput of 0.90, MPG is about 0.28
MFU must first be multiplied by the job's scaling efficiency before it can be compared with Llama 3
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. MFU divides by the time spent on retained steps, so it cannot see capacity the job never held or held time that kept no progress. Only the product of the three factors states how much of the fleet becomes useful work. MFU excludes recomputation, which hardware FLOPs utilization counts, and multiplying fleet MFU by scaling efficiency would charge exposed time twice.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate why a high MFU does not establish efficient use of the fleet.

questions.question: A serving replica's batch-one decode step runs at about 0.3% of its FP16 peak against a bandwidth floor of about 5.2 ms per token. A new accelerator doubles peak FP16 arithmetic at the same memory bandwidth. What does the iron law predict for this step?
choices: Decode time halves to about 2.6 ms per token
Decode time falls by about 0.3%, the share of peak the step uses
MBU halves, because more arithmetic capacity lowers bandwidth efficiency
The 5.2 ms floor is unchanged and MFU halves, because faster arithmetic shortens only the compute term, which is not exposed in this step
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. A higher peak arithmetic rate shortens only the compute term of the iron law, and only where that term is exposed. At the bandwidth floor, the step's time is set by streaming the weight shard, so doubling the peak leaves the time and MBU unchanged and halves MFU. Placing the step's time against the roofline and the Fleet Law terms predicts what a faster device will buy.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the fallacy that more peak FLOP/s proportionally shortens a step.

questions.question: True or False: Moving the running example's training to a lower-precision format with twice the arithmetic throughput would roughly halve its 245 ms fleet step.
questions.answer: False. Faster arithmetic shortens only the local compute work it applies to. About 65 ms of each 245 ms fleet step lies beyond the node baseline, mostly in the exposed data-axis gradient exchange, which faster arithmetic does not touch, and matrix multiplications are only part of local execution. Lower precision can also shrink the bytes each value moves, but the end-to-end gain depends on which exposed intervals change, and the speed counts only if the contract's quality check still passes.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the limits of lower-precision arithmetic on a communication-heavy fleet step.

questions.question: Explain how a job's mean step time can match its plan while intermittent stragglers lower its program goodput, and describe how the chapter's measurement approach exposes them.
questions.answer: A synchronous step ends when its slowest rank finishes, so a rank that falls behind in short episodes, through thermal throttling, a degrading link, or a host pause, delays its whole communication group each time. The mean spreads those episodes into what looks like a small, uniform slowdown, and a trace taken between episodes shows nothing. Continuous per-rank step timers expose the episodes as outliers and trigger a trace of the slow rank beside a healthy peer, while the gray-failure regression tier watches the step-time distribution fleet-wide. Each wait lowers program goodput, whoever decides to replace the node.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why the step-time distribution, not the mean, reveals intermittent straggler losses.

questions.question: Why does a successful compilation not establish that a program is well optimized?
choices: A compiler applies the transformations it implements under its own cost model; derived layouts can insert resharding collectives in every layer, and a shape distribution that forces recompilation shows up as slow retained steps
Compilers optimize only host code, so accelerator kernels are left unchanged
A completed build disables fusion to guarantee numerical safety
Compilation removes all communication, so any remaining loss must come from faulty hardware
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. A completed build does not say which transformations applied. Compiler-derived partitioning inserts a resharding collective wherever two derived layouts disagree, and frequent recompilation in steady operation is a program goodput loss rather than startup. A compiled step is therefore a hypothesis, checked by counting the trace's collectives against the layout's prediction and by measuring program goodput before and after under the contract.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish a successful compilation from verified program goodput.

questions.question: In the running example, scheduling loses 35% of fleet capacity and the program 31%. Explain why a perfect scheduler would add only about 15% of fleet capacity as useful work, and what should decide which lever comes first.
questions.answer: Capacity recovered at the first boundary must still cross the runtime and program boundaries at their current rates, so recovering all 35% yields about $0.35 \times 0.43 \approx 0.15$ of fleet capacity as useful work. At the owners' ceilings, the scheduling lever raises MPG from 0.28 to 0.35 and the program lever to 0.38. The value of one point of each factor, the product of the other two, together with each owner's reachable ceiling, decides the order, not the size of the loss.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why the largest loss share is not the largest recoverable gain.
